This page gathers academic work connected to Statistical Justice and to the broader question of how official data systems recognize, misrecognize, or fail marginalized populations. The papers presented here move between empirical research, conceptual development, and policy relevance, with a particular focus on gender identity, civil registration, vital statistics, and official data infrastructures.
When death tears you apart: the omission of transgender identities in Colombian death certificates # Authors: [Insert Authors] | Year: 2025 | Journal: International Journal for Transgender Health
This peer-reviewed article examines how transgender identities are erased in Colombia’s death registration system and what that erasure means for dignity, public health, and institutional recognition. Based on qualitative interviews with transgender and non-binary community leaders across Colombia, the paper shows how administrative practices can extend exclusion beyond death itself, and argues that recognizing gender identity in death certificates is both a human rights issue and a matter of health equity.
Read article When Populations Are Not Counted: Statistical Justice and Gender-Identity Data in Colombia’s Official Statistics # Authors: [Insert Authors] | Year: 2026 | Journal: Data and Policy (Under Review)
This manuscript introduces Statistical Justice as a framework for understanding how official statistics can reproduce or challenge inequality. Drawing on Colombia’s gender-identity data ecosystem, it examines the gap between legal recognition and everyday data practice, and argues that inclusion in official statistics must be designed in ways that enable recognition, redistribution, and protection.

Cuando la muerte te destroza: La omisión de las identidades trans en los certificados de defunción en Colombia # Policy Brief This policy brief, based on the published article in the International Journal of Transgender Health, presents the study’s main findings in a more accessible and action-oriented format. It highlights the barriers that trans and non-binary people face in death registration, and calls for changes in the civil registration and vital statistics system.
View policy brief in Spanish Hacia la inclusión de identidades de género diversas en las estadísticas vitales en Colombia # Technical Note This technical review maps the legal, institutional, and policy landscape for including diverse gender identities in Colombia’s vital statistics. It identifies major bottlenecks, recent advances, and possible pathways for reform, including standards, interoperability, legal change, and participatory design.

This series explores the human stories behind Statistical Justice, the people, absences, and institutional failures that often remain hidden in official data. Through short films, the project seeks to bring together questions of recognition, identity, violence, and public memory in a more intimate and narrative form.
Currently in development. We are seeking support to produce the full series. Episode 1: Death Certificates (Teaser)
The first episode begins with memory: a trans woman remembering friends who have died, and the fear of what happens when no one is left to insist, this is who she was.
From there, the film opens onto a deeper question: how identity can be lost, rewritten, or erased in official records after death — and why that loss is not only personal, but institutional.

The right to be recognized in government systems, and for official data to reflect the true diversity of societies. A framework developed from work in Colombia and designed to travel across contexts.
Explore the framework Read the research The Problem # Statistical Justice emerged from work in Colombia with transgender communities, and was developed as part of the work of Liga de Salud Trans. It grew from a simple but urgent problem: many trans people are not properly recognized in the official systems meant to count them.
In official records, people may be registered under the wrong name, the wrong gender, or in ways that fail to reflect who they were. This is not just a technical mistake. It is a deeper failure of recognition and governance. When official data does not reflect people as they are, inequality becomes harder to trace, public action harder to shape, and institutional harm easier to overlook.
While the framework was born from this work in Colombia, it was designed to travel. Statistical Justice offers a way to think across contexts, populations, and data systems about what happens when recognition fails — and what it would take for official data to more fully reflect the diversity of societies.
The Work # **The Framework** An introduction to the concept of statistical justice, its dimensions, and the key ideas that shape the framework.
**Research and Publications** Academic papers, technical documents, policy briefs, and public writing that explore these questions in Colombia and beyond.

title: The Book

content:
Statistical Justice is a framework for thinking about what official data systems owe to the populations they count. Developed from work in Colombia and designed to travel across contexts, it argues that just statistical governance requires recognition, redistribution, and protection, not one without the others.
Official statistical systems do more than describe society. They shape who becomes visible to the state, under what categories, and with what consequences for rights, resources, and recognition. When those systems exclude, misclassify, or distort the lives of marginalized populations, the effects are not only technical. They are political, institutional, and deeply human.
What is Statistical Justice? # The right to be recognized in government systems, and for official data to reflect the true diversity of societies. This means more than being counted. A population can appear in official records and still be misrepresented through categories that distort its reality, erase important dimensions of identity, or fail to reflect how people understand themselves. Statistical Justice starts from the idea that representation in official data is not just a technical result. It is a matter of governance, dignity, and justice.
The Three Dimensions # The framework is organized around three connected dimensions: recognition, redistribution, and protection. Together, they help explain not only how statistical injustice happens, but also what more just statistical governance would require.
Recognition # Recognition means being represented in an accurate and self-determined way, free from pathologizing or distorting categories. Statistical Justice argues that inclusion alone is not enough. The categories used should be developed in ways that respect dignity, lived experience, and the participation of the populations they describe.
Redistribution # Redistribution asks whether statistical visibility leads to material consequences in the world. Visibility does not automatically produce justice. Statistical Justice treats redistribution as a core part of what just representation requires, ensuring visibility translates into better services and fairer policies.
Protection # Protection means that populations must be included under conditions that do not increase their exposure to surveillance, discrimination, or harm. Protection is not a limit on inclusion; it is a condition for it.
Two Key Concepts # The framework also introduces two key concepts that help explain why statistical injustice persists even in contexts where legal recognition has advanced.
Legal-statistical decoupling
How can legal recognition exist without statistical recognition?
This describes the structural gap between legal recognition and statistical reform. A population may gain rights under the law, while the official statistical systems that shape collective visibility remain unchanged.
The visibility-protection paradox
What happens when visibility is offered without protection?
This captures a central tension: becoming more visible can also mean becoming more vulnerable. Inclusion in official systems may support access or policy response, but it can also create exposure to surveillance or discrimination. Real visibility requires protection.
Statistical Justice offers a way to name a structural problem, understand how it works, and imagine what more just statistical systems might require.
